Pour
pore
v.t. (rendering Hebrew shaphak/yatsaq, Greek ekcheō)
Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Welsh bwrw, to cast or shed. Hebrew shaphak is to pour out, spill, or shed — used of blood, of wrath, of the soul in prayer — and yatsaq is to pour as one pours oil in anointing. Both keep the idea of emptying a vessel completely.

Biblical Definition

Pouring in Scripture is emptying without reserve, and it is used of God and of men in ways that answer one another. God pours out His Spirit: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), the prophecy Peter claimed at Pentecost. He pours out blessing beyond capacity: “prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Malachi 3:10). The Servant pours out Himself: “he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12) — the atonement described as a vessel emptied to the last. And the believer is invited to do the one thing he can: “Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). The pattern is worth marking. Every pouring in Scripture is total — the Spirit not measured out, the blessing beyond room, the soul unto death, the heart held back in nothing — and the reserve that characterises most religion is exactly what the word excludes.

Webster 1828 Definition

To cause to flow out of a vessel; to send forth in a stream; to empty out. In Scripture, God pouring out His Spirit upon all flesh, pouring out a blessing beyond room to receive it, the Servant pouring out His soul unto death, and the believer commanded to pour out his heart before God.

expand to see more

POUR, v.t. 1. To cause to flow, as a liquid; to send forth from a vessel.

2. To emit; to send forth in a stream or continued succession.

3. To send forth freely; as, to pour out one's complaint or one's heart.

4. Perhaps from the Welsh bwrw, to cast, to shed; Hebrew shaphak, to pour out.

5. In Scripture, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, Joel 2; he hath poured out his soul unto death, Isa. 53.

Key Scripture

Joel 2:28 — "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:"

Malachi 3:10 — "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it."

Isaiah 53:12 — "Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

Psalm 62:8 — "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah."

Modern Corruption

The outpouring of the Spirit is claimed as a repeatable event men can schedule, and Malachi's promise of poured-out blessing is converted into a contract by which giving obliges God to enrich the giver.

expand to see more

Malachi 3:10 has become the most-quoted verse in prosperity preaching, and the abuse is worth stating precisely, because the verse does teach something real. God addresses a nation under a covenant with tangible sanctions, charges it with robbing Him in tithes and offerings, and promises agricultural blessing on repentance — opened windows, a rebuked devourer, a fruitful vine. What the prosperity teacher does is lift the promise out of that covenant, attach it to individual giving in a new-covenant church, and guarantee financial return in proportion to the gift. That is not faith but investment, and it makes God a debtor to men. Scripture's new-covenant teaching on giving is different in kind: give cheerfully, not grudgingly nor of necessity; sow bountifully and God will supply seed to the sower; and the God who did not spare His own Son will freely give us all things — none of which is a mechanism for enrichment.

The outpouring of the Spirit suffers a parallel corruption. Joel's prophecy was claimed by Peter at Pentecost as fulfilled — this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel — and the Spirit poured out then has not been withdrawn. Modern revivalism repeatedly announces fresh outpourings, schedules them, and markets them, as though Pentecost were a recurring event the church could arrange. The cessationist position the dictionary holds is not that God has stopped working powerfully, but that the sign gifts attesting the apostolic foundation have ceased with the foundation, and that the Spirit now works through the ordinary means He has appointed. The principle to recover is Psalm 62:8, which is available to any believer on any day: pour out your heart before Him, holding nothing back, for God is a refuge for us.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaphak, to pour out, spill, or shed; yatsaq, to pour as oil in anointing; 'arah, to empty out; Greek ekcheō, to pour out.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out or shed; used of blood shed, of wrath poured out, and of the soul poured out in prayer (1 Samuel 1:15).

Hebrew yatsaq (H3332) — to pour or cast; the verb of anointing oil poured on the head (1 Samuel 10:1).

Hebrew 'arah (H6168) — to make bare, to empty out; “he hath poured out his soul unto death” (Isaiah 53:12).

Greek ekcheō (G1632) — to pour out; used of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:17-18).

Greek spendō (G4689) — to be poured out as a drink offering; Paul's word for his own approaching death (2 Timothy 4:6).

Usage

"Of the promised gift of the Spirit: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2:28)."

"Of the atonement as total self-giving: he hath poured out his soul unto death (Isaiah 53:12)."

"Of prayer without reserve: ye people, pour out your heart before him (Psalm 62:8)."
